The story relies heavily on subtext, which naturally enriches both the setting and the emotional depth of the relationship between the mother (Ilse) and her estranged son (Jonas) without feeling forced. 

On the surface, the two are simply crossing a river on an old ferry and making sparse small talk about the boat's motor, Jonas's gray hair, and a school group arriving on Friday. However, the subtext reveals a deep emotional distance, grief over the death of the father (Henning), and the quiet decay of their rural home. 

For example, the setting of the ferry and its sputtering motor serves as a subtextual metaphor for Ilse herself and her way of life. When Jonas remarks at the beginning that the motor sounds like it is about to fall apart, and looks at the surroundings "like an appraisal" (*wie ein Gutachten*), the subtext shows his concern that his aging mother can no longer manage this life alone. When Ilse insists at the very end on driving him right back across the river just "so you see that nothing is falling apart," she isn't just defending the mechanical state of the boat—she is fiercely defending her own resilience, independence, and refusal to give up the life she shared with her late husband. 

Additionally, small physical details enrich the setting and characterization through subtext: Jonas's rolling suitcase (showing he has become an outsider from the city) and his holding onto the railing during a calm crossing (showing he has lost his childhood familiarity with the river) subtly highlight the time and distance that have grown between them.
